extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, platform designers, policymakers, and practitioners interested in crowdsourcing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for designing, selecting, and assessing crowdsourcing approaches and projects across domains (research, journalism, product design, public policy, AI training, etc.). Covers methods, success factors, quality/ethical considerations, and governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages of using crowdsourcing
rubrics_metrics.description: Advantages of using crowdsourcing include lowered costs, improved speed, improved quality, increased flexibility, and/or increased scalability of the work, as well as promoting diversity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these expected benefits when justifying or evaluating a crowdsourcing approach; verify empirically (costs, speed, quality). Beware of overstating benefits — results vary by domain and design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowdsourcing methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowdsourcing methods include competitions, virtual labor markets, open online collaboration and data donation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select method based on goals: competitions for ideation/innovation, virtual labor markets (e.g., MTurk) for microtasks, open collaboration for collective resources, and data donation for passively contributed datasets. Each method has different governance, incentive, and quality implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Task suitability / task complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Although crowdsourcing complicated tasks can be difficult, simple work tasks can be crowdsourced cheaply and effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate task decomposition, need for expertise, and whether tasks are easily parallelizable. If a task is complex, consider hybrid models, expert vetting, or alternate methods rather than pure crowdsourcing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform design: user communication and presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of user communication and platform presentation can have a major bearing on the success of an online crowdsourcing project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design clear interfaces, communication channels, and presentation of tasks/ideas; test presentation effects. Poor presentation or communication can depress participation and idea quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant motivation and incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the public submit solutions that are then owned by the entity who originally broadcast the problem. In some cases, the contributor of the solution is compensated monetarily with prizes or public recognition. In other cases, the only rewards may be praise or intellectual satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose incentives (money, recognition, intrinsic rewards) consistent with participant motivations. Empirical work (e.g., studies on Mechanical Turk motivations) should guide incentive levels and non-monetary rewards to sustain engagement and quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership / compensation model clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the public submit solutions that are then owned by the entity who originally broadcast the problem. In some cases, the contributor of the solution is compensated monetarily with prizes or public recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make IP and compensation terms explicit before participation. Evaluate ethical and legal implications (ownership transfer, royalties, moral rights) and potential participant backlash if unclear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-based typology — Knowledge discovery and management
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge discovery and management is used for information management problems where an organization mobilizes a crowd to find and assemble information. It is ideal for creating collective resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when goal is assembling or discovering dispersed information (e.g., databases, encyclopedias). Ensure curation and verification mechanisms to maintain quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-based typology — Distributed human intelligence tasking (HIT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distributed human intelligence tasking (HIT) is used for information management problems where an organization has a set of information in hand and mobilizes a crowd to process or analyze the information. It is ideal for processing large data sets that computers cannot easily do. Amazon Mechanical Turk uses this approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use HITs for microtasks like labeling, transcription, or simple judgments. Implement redundancy, attention checks, and quality-control pipelines to mitigate low-quality or automated responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-based typology — Broadcast search
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcast search is used for ideation problems where an organization mobilizes a crowd to come up with a solution to a problem that has an objective, provable right answer. It is ideal for scientific problem-solving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when a clear objective solution exists (e.g., algorithmic or technical problems). Provide clear evaluation criteria, prize structures, and adjudication processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-based typology — Peer-vetted creative production
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer-vetted creative production is used for ideation problems, where an organization mobilizes a crowd to come up with a solution to a problem which has an answer that is subjective or dependent on public support. It is ideal for design, aesthetic, or policy problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine open submission with community voting/feedback; plan for governance of voting, manipulation risks, and mechanisms to surface high-quality subjective contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit vs implicit crowdsourcing
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowdsourcing can either take an explicit or an implicit route: Explicit crowdsourcing lets users work together to evaluate, share, and build different specific tasks, while implicit crowdsourcing means that users solve a problem as a side effect of something else they are doing. Implicit crowdsourcing can be standalone or piggyback (piggyback takes users' information from a third-party website).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether participation is voluntary/visible (explicit) or a by-product (implicit). Respect consent and transparency for implicit approaches (piggyback/data donation) and evaluate data provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Success conditions for social media fact-checking / community notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowdsourcing on such platforms is thought to be effective in combating partisan misinformation on social media when certain conditions are met. Success may depend on trust in fact-checking sources, the ability to present information that challenges previous beliefs without causing excessive dissonance, and having a sufficiently large and diverse crowd of participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For platform-based fact-checking, cultivate trusted sources, design messaging to reduce defensive rejection, and recruit a diverse cross-ideological participant base. Monitor for echo-chambers and coordinate cross-community outreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowd size and diversity requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective crowdsourcing interventions must have a sufficiently large and diverse crowd of participants; leveraging network analysis to connect users with neighboring communities outside their ideological echo chambers can improve outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess target population coverage and diversity metrics; if crowd is small or homogeneous, results may be biased or ineffective. Use outreach and stratified recruitment to increase representativeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data quality controls and worker screening (research use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers have used crowdsourcing systems such as Amazon Mechanical Turk to aid their research projects; crowdsourcing systems provided researchers with the ability to gather large amounts of data. However, concerns exist about bots, inattentive humans, and low-quality data — quality management on MTurk and other platforms is documented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement pre-screening, attention checks, redundancy, gold-standard items, platform-approved samples (e.g., CloudResearch Approved Group), and statistical checks for bots/inattentive behavior. Report recruitment and quality-control procedures in research outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical compensation and labor standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussions include ethical and practical considerations for compensation of crowdsourced research participants and critiques of crowdsourcing as potential exploitation of consumer work; labour law and fair pay considerations arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate pay against local wage standards, consider fair compensation, and document ethical review/consent. Be mindful of labor-law implications and platform-specific worker protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matching participant expertise to task
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowdsourcing may produce solutions from amateurs or volunteers, from experts, or from small businesses — composition affects performance and suitability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define required skill levels and recruit appropriate participant segments; for expert tasks, use targeted calls, vetting, or hybrid expert–crowd pipelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common failure modes / reasons crowdsourcing fails
rubrics_metrics.description: Research identifies reasons crowdsourcing fails (e.g., poor matching of problem to crowd, inadequate incentives, platform design issues, coordination friction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnose risk factors before launch: unclear problem framing, weak incentives, deficient quality control, lack of governance. Build mitigation: clearer framing, pilot tests, iterative design, and robust incentive structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governance rules and thresholds (example: Lego Ideas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: Lego Ideas requires a submitted product to receive 10,000 votes before it will be formally reviewed in stages and go into production; the creator receives royalties. Governance and review thresholds shape outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design transparent governance (voting thresholds, review stages, reward mechanics). Ensure thresholds are appropriate to scale and that review processes are resourced to follow through.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data donation: consent, provenance, and use cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Data donation is a crowdsourcing approach where participants volunteer their authentic digital profile information for research projects; examples include Mozilla Rally and DataSkop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize informed consent, anonymization, provenance tracking, and ethical oversight. Be explicit about uses and risks; verify legal compliance for cross-jurisdictional data collection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregation and statistical frameworks for quality (gold-standard creation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: combining expert diagnoses with those from minimally trained individuals to create a gold standard library (malaria diagnosis project) using a statistical framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use aggregation models (weighted voting, expert anchoring, statistical combination) to produce reliable labels; validate aggregated outputs against independent expert sets and report uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem framing and topic selection that attract participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful crowdsourcing themes include problems that bug people, things that make people feel good about themselves, projects that tap into niche knowledge of proud experts, and subjects that people find sympathetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame calls to action around emotional salience, identity, or intrinsic rewards. Target outreach to niche expert communities when specialized knowledge is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain-specific suitability and use-cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowdsourcing is applied across domains (astronomy, ornithology, seismology, journalism, public policy, healthcare, product design, energy systems, genealogy, language data, etc.) with different success criteria and needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or designing a project, map domain-specific needs (e.g., verification intensity in journalism; clinical validation in healthcare; reproducibility in science) and adapt methods, incentives, and QC accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scalability and ability to process large datasets
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowdsourcing has been used to provide researchers the ability to gather large amounts of data, and to process large datasets that computers cannot easily do (e.g., labeling, OCR corrections, image identification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether crowdsourcing scales cost-effectively for dataset size and timeline; use task batching, parallelization, and automated pre-processing to improve efficiency.
